title: You Were Afraid of My Mortal Flesh
text:
You were afraid of my mortal flesh, and in it you sought

the immortal soul. To find it, with harsh words

you opened great wounds in me.

Then you bent over them and breathed in,

terrible, the scent of my blood.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the clinical violence of a spiritual search enacted upon the woman's body.

title: The Rosebush's Restlessness
text:
The rosebush, in its restless way of flowering,

burns through the sap that nourishes its being.

Look at the roses falling from the tree:

there are so many, it will die of this disease!

The rosebush is not grown; its impatient life

consumes itself by flowering before its time.
editorial_note: The botanical allegory retains its feverish expenditure; rosal is varied as bush and tree only where English cadence requires.

title: Listen: I Was Like a Sleeping Sea…
text:
Listen: I was like a sleeping sea.

You woke me, and the tempest broke loose.

I shake my waves, I sink my ships,

I climb to heaven and punish stars,

I grow ashamed and hide within my folds,

I go mad and kill my fish.

Do not look at me in fear. This is what you wanted.
editorial_note: The sea remains both speaker and body; the clipped verbs preserve the storm's escalating self-destruction.

title: Complaint
text:
Lord, this is my complaint—

you will understand:

I am dying of love,

but I cannot love.


I pursue perfection

in myself and everyone;

I pursue perfection

so that I might love.


I am consumed in my own fire.

Lord, mercy, mercy!

I am dying of love,

but I cannot love!
editorial_note: The prayer's plain repetition and impossible contradiction are retained without ornamental expansion.

title: And You?
text:
Yes, I move, I live, I make mistakes;

like running, mingling water, I feel

the savage vertigo of motion:

I breathe the forests, touch new earth.


Yes, I move; perhaps I go in search

of suns, dawns, tempest, and oblivion.

What are you doing there, so wretched and polished?

You are the stone beside which I pass.
editorial_note: The speaker's mobile, imperfect vitality is set against the addressee's polished lifelessness.

title: Parasites
text:
I never thought that God could have a form.

Absolute his life; absolute his law.

He never had eyes: he sees through the stars.

He never had hands: he strikes with the seas.

He never had a tongue: he speaks through lightning.

I will tell you—do not be astonished;

I know he has parasites: all things, and humankind.
editorial_note: The aphoristic theology remains severe, and the final colon preserves the poem's satirical revelation.

title: Peace
text:
Let us go toward the trees… sleep

will come into us by celestial grace.

Let us go toward the trees; the night

will be tender to us, sorrow light.


Let us go toward the trees, the soul

drowsing on the wildwood scent.

But hush, do not speak, be merciful;

do not wake the sleeping birds.
editorial_note: The invitation moves from human grief into woodland quiet; virtue becomes grace to preserve its spiritual agency.

title: Appearance
text:
I live within four mathematical walls,

aligned to the meter. I am ringed by listless

little souls who do not know the slightest thing

of this blue fever feeding my chimera.


I wear a counterfeit skin, striped in gray.

A crow that guards a fleur-de-lis beneath its wing.

My fierce and sullen beak provokes a certain laughter:

I think myself pure farce and hindrance.
editorial_note: The constrained geometry and self-fashioned disguise retain their tension with the hidden blue fever.

title: Ancestral Weight
text:
You told me: my father never wept;

you told me: my grandfather never wept;

the men of my bloodline never wept—

they were made of steel.


As you spoke, a tear welled up

and fell into my mouth… more poison.

Never have I drunk from another cup so small.


Weak woman, poor woman who understands:

I knew the pain of centuries as I drank it.

Oh, my soul cannot bear

all its weight!
editorial_note: The inherited masculine prohibition becomes bodily poison; bloodline keeps raza familial rather than racialized.

title: Little Man
text:
Little man, little man,

set your canary free—it wants to fly…

I am the canary, little man;

let me leap away.

I was in your cage, little man,

little man who gives me a cage.

I call you little because you do not understand me,

and never will.

Nor do I understand you; but meanwhile,

open up the cage—I want to escape.

Little man, I loved you for half an hour;

do not ask me for more.
editorial_note: The diminutive is kept as both belittlement and refrain, with the caged voice remaining sharp and unsentimental.
